newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: China not ready yet to okay Guatemala peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: China not ready yet to okay Guatemala peacekeepers.

text.p: Despite a recent peace treaty signalling the end of Guatemala's long-running guerrilla war, the U.N. Security Council on Tuesday was unable to approve 155 peacekeepers to oversee disarmament provisions of the accord.
China remained the solo holdout on the resolution, introduced and discussed during a closed-door council session, because of Guatemala's ties with Taiwan, which Beijing considers a renegade province.
The resolution would authorise U.N. military observers for three months as part of a U.N.-brokered peace plan signed on Dec. 29 in Guatemala City.

But diplomats said they did not expect Beijing to veto the measure when it finally comes to a vote. They speculated that China wanted to wring some concessions from Guatemala first, perhaps a high-level visit and an eventual trade mission to wean the Central American country slowly from Taiwan.
Guatemala receives considerable economic aid from Taiwan.
Chinese spokesman Chen Ranfeng said Guatemala's ties with Taiwan and its invitation to Taiwan's Foreign Ministry to attend the Dec. 29 events were an affront to Beijing.

"We have told them several times and it seems to us they haven't given us a very positive response so far," he told reporters. "I am wondering when they have to give us positive response to redress this issue."

He said the position of Guatemala, a country of six million people, harmed the sovereignty and territorial integrity of China. "We just want them to show their respect to the sovereignty of China and the feelings of the Chinese people, because this is very important to us," he said.
Chen said consultations were ongoing on Guatemala, adding: "We will keep our fingers crossed."

A similar pattern emerged each time peacekeepers for Haiti were due for approval. China threatened to veto the contingents because of Haiti's relations with Taiwan, but approval was eventually given for a reduced number of troops following visits to Haiti from Chinese envoys.

More than 100,000 people have died in Guatemala's 36-year armed conflict, the last in Central America, and a further 40,000 have "disappeared," with the army having been accused of human rights abuses against indigenous people.

Under military provisions of the peace accord, Guatemala's army will redeploy units to specified locations after which troops from the rebel Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) move to eight assembly points.

URNG leader Ricardo Ramirez, who is known by his nom de guerre, Rolando Moran, said last Friday he was waiting for the United Nations to establish the day when the former guerrillas would move to the assembly points.

The unarmed U.N. military observers are to verify a ceasefire and patrol a security zone around each assembly point. The guerrillas eventually are to hand over their weapons and uniforms to Guatemalan and U.N. personnel before leaving assembly points.
